title: The siddur
hookLine: the prayer book, named "order", the most-used Jewish book after the Torah

cards: Near the door of a synagogue there's often a shelf of matching books, worn soft at the corners.

One page carries a wine stain from a holiday, another a child's pencil mark, another the crease of a hand that held it for a lifetime. People take one on the way in without thinking. It isn't the Torah scroll.
But for a Jew who prays every day, it may be the book held more often than any other. For the next stretch of this year, this path walks through it, in order.

teach.b: The word is siddur. It comes from seder, order, the same root as the Passover seder, the ordered meal.
A siddur is the prayer book: the weekday prayers, the Sabbath and festival prayers, blessings for food and for waking up, all arranged in the order they're said. That order is the point.
Jewish prayer isn't mostly a blank page.
It has a shape: blessings, then psalms, then the Shema, then the standing prayer, then the closing. The Talmud discusses many of these prayers long before anyone bound them into one volume.
Among the oldest written orders of prayer that survive are two from the geonim, the heads of the academies in Babylonia: the order of Rav Amram Gaon, and the siddur of Rav Saadia Gaon.
Since then, many versions have grown. Ashkenazi Jews, from Central and Eastern Europe, have their rite. Sephardi and Mizrahi Jews, from Spain, North Africa and the Middle East, have theirs.
Yemenite communities, Hasidic communities and the modern movements each have siddurim of their own. The core is shared; the details differ, and each community keeps its own.
Why give prayer an order at all? One answer: on the days you have no words, the siddur has them. On the days you have too many, it gives them a path.
Starting tomorrow, it opens, step by step.

how: Jews who pray daily use a siddur for the morning, afternoon and evening services, and a related book, the machzor, for the High Holy Days. Different communities follow different rites (nusach), such as Ashkenaz, Sefard and Edot HaMizrach.

practice: If you have a siddur, take it off the shelf, feel its weight, and open it anywhere to read one line, in Hebrew or in translation.
If you don't, hold any book you've gone back to many times, and remember that people have prayed these words, in this order, from books like this, across many generations.
